about.title: Roots and Rational Exponents
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. There are two ideas: simplifying roots, then fractional exponents. Each gets about 15 minutes, with a check question after every step. Pause at any question and take as long as you need.

sources.title: 8.1 Simplify Expressions with Roots, Intermediate Algebra 2e
High School: Number and Quantity (Common Core State Standards for Mathematics)
1.3 Radicals and Rational Exponents, College Algebra 2e
8.NS.A.1: Rational and Irrational Numbers and Repeating Decimals
HSN.RN.A.1: Why Rational Exponents Mean Roots

say.text: Last class you met zero and negative exponents. Today we meet roots, and then a surprise: a root is secretly an exponent.
First, the square root. Picture 9 blocks packed into a square. It is 3 blocks across and 3 blocks down.

show.text: 9 blocks make a 3 by 3 square, so the square root of 9 is 3

say.text: A square root answers one question: what number times itself gives this? Both 13 and −13 work for 169. The radical sign √ means only the positive one.

show.text: √169 = 13 (the positive root; the radical sign means positive)

ask.why: 7 × 7 = 49. The radical sign √ asks for the positive root only, so the answer is just 7. (−7 also squares to 49, but √ does not mean that one.)

say.text: Some squares are worth knowing by heart. In 8th grade you evaluated roots of small perfect squares. Here are the ones to keep handy.
Cube roots work the same way, with three copies. Cubed means 3 × 3 × 3. A cube root asks which number, used three times, makes this.
A cube root can handle negatives, because a negative times a negative times a negative is negative. So ∛(−27) = −3. A square root of a negative number is not a real number.

wrong: It is not a real number
ask.why: (−2) × (−2) × (−2) = −8. Cube roots of negative numbers are real. Only square roots of negatives are not real.

say.text: Now two kinds of numbers. √36 = 6 is a whole number, so it is rational. √2 is different. Its decimal never ends and never repeats.

show.text: Rational: decimal ends or repeats (√36 = 6) | Irrational: never ends, never repeats (√2 = 1.41421356…)

say.text: The rule of thumb: the square root of a whole number that is not a perfect square is irrational. √5 and √50 are examples.

ask.why: 16, 25 and 100 are perfect squares (4, 5 and 10), so those roots are whole numbers. 20 is not a perfect square, so √20 is irrational.

say.text: You can place an irrational root on the number line by squeezing it between two perfect squares. √30 sits between √25 and √36.

ask.q: Between which two whole numbers is √30?
ask.why: 5² = 25 and 6² = 36, and 30 is between them. So √30 is between 5 and 6.

say.text: Now simplifying. There is a rule for roots of products: √(ab) = √a · √b, when a and b are not negative.
A square root is simplified when nothing inside it is a perfect-square factor. We use the rule to pull those factors out.

show.text: 1. Find the largest perfect-square factor. 2. Rewrite the number as a product. 3. Take the root of the perfect square.

say.text: Try √50. 25 is a perfect square and 25 × 2 = 50. So √50 = √25 · √2 = 5√2. The whole number goes in front.
Your turn. Look for the largest perfect square that divides 72.

ask.why: 72 = 36 × 2, and 36 is the largest perfect-square factor. √36 = 6, so √72 = 6√2. 2√18 and 3√8 are equal in value but still have a perfect square inside (9 and 4). 36√2 forgets to take the root of 36.

say.text: Why bother? Say a game sprite is a square with an area of 48 square pixels. Its side is √48 = √(16 · 3) = 4√3, about 6.9 pixels.

show.text: A square game sprite with area 48 square pixels; one side labelled 4√3, about 6.9 pixels

say.text: Cube roots simplify the same way, but you look for perfect cubes: 8, 27, 64, 125. Try ∛54. Since 27 × 2 = 54, we get ∛54 = 3∛2.
Second idea: fractional exponents. Remember that a power to a power multiplies the exponents. Let's use that rule with a fraction.
So 5^(1/3) is a number that, cubed, gives 5. That is the cube root of 5! We define it that way so exponent rules keep working. Same for 9^(1/2) = 3.
The rule: an exponent of 1/n means the nth root. The bottom number of the fraction tells you which root.

ask.why: The exponent 1/3 means the cube root, and 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. 41.67 comes from dividing 125 by 3, which is not what the exponent means.

say.text: What if the top number isn't 1? Then the top is a power and the bottom is a root. So 8^(2/3) means take the cube root of 8, then square it.
Tip: take the root first. It keeps the numbers small. 4^(3/2) is (√4)³, which is 2³.

ask.why: The bottom number 2 means square root, and √4 = 2. The top number 3 means cube it: 2³ = 8. 6 comes from multiplying 4 × 3 ÷ 2, which is not what an exponent means.

say.text: One caution. An even root, like a square root, of a negative number is not a real number. An odd root, like a cube root, can be negative.

ask.q: Which of these is NOT a real number?
ask.why: No real number times itself gives −9, because a square is never negative. The other three are real: ∛(−8) = −2, √9 = 3 and ∛8 = 2.

say.text: Let's wrap up. A root asks what number gives this when multiplied by itself. Simplify by pulling out perfect squares or cubes. And a fraction in an exponent is a root in disguise.

show.text: √ and ∛ undo squaring and cubing. | √(ab) = √a·√b lets us simplify. | a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a. | a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)^m.

other_side.claim: The symbol √49 means 7 only, not both 7 and −7.
other_side.other_view: The radical sign names only the positive (principal) root. But when you solve an equation such as x² = 49, both 7 and −7 are solutions, and the 8th-grade standard asks students to write such solutions with the root symbol. So the sign decides whether you get one answer or two.

other_side.claim: Rational exponents can be defined for any base whose root is a real number, such as (−8)^(1/3) = −2.
other_side.other_view: Some courses state the exponent properties for positive bases only, because the properties can give odd results with negative bases. That is a safer rule, though it leaves out cases like (−8)^(1/3). Your teacher or test may use either convention.
